entities.summary:
Algiers is the capital and largest city of Algeria, located on the Mediterranean Sea in the north-central portion of the country. With an estimated urban population of 4.3 million (2025), it is the third-largest city in Africa. Algiers sits on a hillside overlooking a broad bay — a geography that gave rise to its Arabic name Al-Jazā'ir ('The Islands'), referring to the offshore islets that the Ottomans used to anchor their naval fortifications.

The site has been continuously inhabited since Phoenician traders founded the colony of Ikosim (c. 4th century BCE). Roman Icosium was a minor settlement; the city grew significantly under Berber Zirid rule (972–1014 CE) and was absorbed into the Hafsid and Zayyanid sultanates. In 1516, the Ottoman privateer Khizr Hayreddin (Barbarossa) invited Ottoman suzerainty to defend against Spanish expansion, transforming Algiers into the most powerful corsair base in the western Mediterranean — the feared Algerian Regency that extracted tribute and ransom from European maritime powers for three centuries.

French forces captured Algiers in June 1830, beginning 132 years of colonial rule that made the city a European-designed showcase of French imperial architecture alongside the ancient casbah (old city). The Casbah of Algiers — an organic Ottoman city of narrow alleys and terraced houses — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and was the main arena of the brutal urban guerrilla warfare during the Battle of Algiers (1957), the most intensely analyzed episode of colonial counter-insurgency in the 20th century.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Algiers played a pivotal role in the Ottoman Empire's expansion into North Africa, with Khizr Hayreddin's invitation in 1516 marking the beginning of Ottoman rule that lasted for nearly four centuries. The city's strategic location and growth under Berber Zirid rule significantly impacted regional trade and politics.
